This may be investigated and discussed in detail. Thus, since antiquity, the Three Teachings have possessed scriptures issued by imperial decree, as recorded in the *Guang hongming ji* (Collection for the Broad Propagation and Elucidation of the Light).
Throughout successive dynasties and reigns, there have been immeasurable titles of such works; these have largely survived without being lost thanks to the emperors and kings who preserved them.

Should there be deficiencies in the textual analysis, the interpretation of meaning, or the historical accounts—these three aspects—let individuals be permitted to investigate and provide detailed corrections and supplements. To rectify what they call the "Buddhas and Patriarchs," if the texts they have examined are indeed erroneous, they must reject them even if they are ancient works;

For although the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Zheng zong ji* (Record of the True Lineage) are both included in the Tripitaka, the two works together comprise a total of forty fascicles.

Examining the names of individuals therein, according to what is recorded in the *Chuan deng lu*, there are one thousand four hundred and thirty-four persons from the time of the Sixth Patriarch downward; whereas according to what is recorded in the *Zheng zong ji*...
Under the Sixth Patriarch, there were one thousand four hundred and ninety-six people.
Among these several thousand individuals, the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) employs only simple prose to record their genealogical succession and biographies;

the *Zheng zong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) likewise uses merely abbreviated brushstrokes to describe their dharma inheritance and lineages. In neither work have more than two thousand people been clearly identified and set forth for posterity.
As for its fundamental tenets, its branching lineages, and its structural outlines and detailed sections, they were so vast and complex that they could not be made known to every household.

Although the texts existed, they did not truly flourish in the world. Fortunately, during the Jingding era of the Song dynasty, there was the Chan Master Dachuang of Lingyin, a man of profound erudition in the Zen school who was born as a manifestation of rare spiritual energy.

Upon examining the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Zheng zong ji* (Record of the True Lineage), one finds that they merely provide a chronological succession of those who received the Dharma, without any distinction between lineages or doctrinal schools.
Consequently, for each individual recorded in the successions of these two works, their respective *yulu* (recorded sayings) have been compiled.
Furthermore, because the Indian patriarchs had prophesied the destinies of Nanyue and Mazu, I have included the records of the "Four Sevens" from India and the "Two Threes" from this land.
Consequently, Nan-yueh was placed at the head and Ch’ing-yüan was appended to the end. This was likely based on the prophecy of Prajñātāra of the Western Heaven.
Furthermore, the *Chuan-teng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) never definitively established that Ch’ing-yüan was the elder and Nan-yueh the younger.
Little did they know that there were eleven other patriarchs preceding Ch’ing-yüan.
The names are present; although Qingyuan is listed before Nanyue, there were eleven others even before Qingyuan who may also be considered his elder brothers.
This sufficiently demonstrates the nature of the two texts, the *Chuan deng lu* and the *Zheng zong ji*.
It merely clarifies the number of individuals and their generational order; it never actually branches into lineages to represent the school’s tenets.

What constitutes the elder brother (*kun*) and what the younger (*ji*)? It is simply composed as a single, undifferentiated form. As the *Jichuan Shipu* (Genealogical Record of Patriarchs and Disciples) states:
"Thus, Master Dachuang determined the seniority of two individuals based on two prophecies, yet later [the text] branched into lineages to represent the school’s tenets."
The first is called the Linji school; the second, the Yunmen school; the third, the Caodong school;
the fourth, the Guiyang school; and the fifth, the Fayan school. Once these five schools were established, their branches and lineages diverged.

Even through thousands of sons and ten thousand grandsons over a hundred billion generations, all shall see that there are schools and lineages, with origins and ramifications. By compiling and collecting the various scriptures, they form one great [tradition].

This compendium of texts establishes a definitive history of the Chan school; its merit is no less than that of Yu. Consequently, for over five hundred years since its circulation, there has been no one who does not praise it as a grand ceremony.

This [work] is as simple and extremely concise as that, yet it is so detailed, clear, and manifest that the difference between them is not merely like that between heaven and earth.
